summary: Bradford's Instagram content on taxes and fiscal policy centers on opposition to property tax increases under Mayor Chow, characterized as cumulatively 25% over three years (7% in 2023, 9.5% in 2024, 6.9% in 2025) without commensurate service improvements. Bradford opposes drawing $512M from reserve funds, characterizing it as unsustainable and likely to force a roughly 10.5% tax increase the following year. Bradford supports property tax cuts for industrial properties and small businesses (proposing a 25% cut funded by the tax stabilization reserve during trade-war conditions), opposes the Vacant Home Tax, the luxury home land transfer tax, and additional housing-related taxes. Bradford also supports open tendering to save an estimated $200M annually, a live music venue tax subclass, and pursuing a new fiscal deal with senior governments. The recurring frame is "paying more, getting less" and demand for value-for-money.

key_positions.stance: Opposes property tax increases above the rate of inflation, characterizing Mayor Chow's cumulative increases as roughly 25% over three years without matching service improvements.
Opposes drawing large sums from the tax stabilization reserve to balance the operating budget, arguing it pushes larger tax bills to future years.
Supports using the tax stabilization reserve during declared emergencies such as a US trade war to fund targeted business tax relief.
Supports cutting property taxes for industrial properties and small businesses (proposing 25% cuts).
Opposes the Vacant Home Tax, characterizing it as a failed program and a tax grab, and supports suspending or shelving it.
Opposes the Mayor's luxury home tax (increased land transfer tax on homes over $3M) and additional taxes on housing.
Supports open tendering for city construction contracts as a way to save an estimated $200M annually.
Supports pursuing a new/more sustainable fiscal deal with federal and provincial governments for Toronto.
Supports a property tax subclass for live music venues offering up to 50% reduction.
Supports value-for-money spending, finding efficiencies, and opposes what he characterizes as pet projects and cost overruns (e.g., $150M bike lane, $965K square renaming).
